findings.paper_title: 8. Housing Enforcement and Civil Penalty Policies
findings.headline: Civil penalties carry a 15% discount for payment within the notice period
findings.detail: The Civil Penalty Policy says that a penalty paid in full within the period specified in the final notice, normally 28 days, will receive a 15% discount. The discount is not extended by an appeal. The paper gives an example where a £16,000 penalty would be paid as £13,600.
findings.matters: The discount reduces the cash actually collected from each penalty, which affects the income a council can plan around from civil penalties.
findings.figures: 15% (prompt payment discount); £16,000 (example penalty); £13,600 (example discounted payment); 28 days (normal payment period)

findings.headline: Unpaid enforcement costs are to be registered as local land charges where legislation permits
findings.detail: Section 1.13 says that where costs remain unpaid, the council will use statutory recovery mechanisms, including registering charges against the property as a local land charge where legislation permits. Section 1.12 adds a bespoke calculator to record officer time and calculate recoverable expenses.
findings.matters: Charges secured against property affect the position of anyone holding or lending against the property, and show how a council is securing cost recovery.

findings.matters: A ring-fence determines whether penalty receipts can offset enforcement costs, which is relevant to how other councils structure this income.

findings.headline: Council maintained deliberately under-borrowed position of £58.4m below Capital Financing Requirement (£236.5m CFR vs £178.1m borrowing)
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying measure of capital borrowing need) was £236.5m but gross external borrowing was only £178.1m. This £58.4m gap reflects deliberate under-borrowing strategy using internal cash reserves to defer expensive long-term borrowing while rates remain elevated. This approach has trade-offs: it defers costs but uses up cash buffers and creates reinvestment risk when balances must eventually be rebuilt.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing is a tactical timing strategy with medium-term risk: it reduces current-year debt costs but locks in higher refinancing requirement later; lenders track whether councils can sustain this position or face forced borrowing at inopportune rates.

findings.headline: Winter 2026 caused significant pothole formation surge; Council allocating £168k innovation budget for new prevention and response methods
findings.detail: Prolonged winter freezing followed by sustained rainfall significantly accelerated surface deterioration and pothole formation. The council is responding with a £168,210 innovation programme to develop and trial new technologies and methods for pothole prevention and response. Further scrutiny review of equipment trials is scheduled before any permanent implementation of new working methods.
findings.matters: Finance officers at councils facing similar pothole pressures would want to know how peers are addressing the issue. This shows one council responding to emerging service demand through efficiency innovation rather than requesting additional funding.
findings.figures: £168,210 allocated to preventative maintenance technology and innovation trial
findings.quote: Winter 2026 caused a significant increase in pothole formation and repairs on local highways. Prolonged freezing conditions, followed by sustained heavy rainfall, have significantly accelerated surface deterioration and pothole formation.

findings.paper_title: 9. Highway and Transport Capital Programme Cabinet Report
findings.headline: £17.4m highways capital programme is fully funded and requires no additional borrowing beyond that already reflected in Council's Treasury Management and Capital Strategies
findings.detail: The 2026/27 programme totals £17,438,155. Funding comprises £4.516m Highways Maintenance grant, £7.317m Local Transport Grant, £5.034m carried forward from 2025/26, and £400,000 corporate allocation. The council explicitly confirms no new borrowing is required for delivery.
findings.matters: For lenders and peer finance officers, this demonstrates the council is managing a substantial capital programme within available resources without increasing debt levels.
findings.figures: £17,438,155 total; £4.516m Highways Maintenance grant; £7.317m Local Transport Grant; £5.034m carried forward; £400,000 corporate allocation
findings.quote: The programme is fully funded within the Council's approved Capital Investment Programme and does not require any additional borrowing beyond that already reflected within the Council's Treasury Management and Capital Strategies.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Debt interest costs budgeted at £9.68m in 2026/27 on average debt of £220m at 4.40% average rate
findings.detail: The council budgets debt interest payments of £9.680m for 2026/27, based on forecast average debt portfolio of £220m at 4.40% average interest rate. Investment income is budgeted at just £0.350m, creating a net financing cost that reflects the council's position as a significant borrower in an elevated rate environment.
findings.matters: High debt service cost relative to minimal investment income shows limited reserve offset; debt costs are substantially above historic levels and create significant revenue commitment.
findings.figures: Debt interest budget £9.680m; investment income budget £0.350m; average debt £220m; average rate 4.40%
findings.quote: The budget for investment income in 2026/27 is £0.350 million. The budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27 is £9.680 million, based on an average debt portfolio of £220 million at an average interest rate of 4.40%.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Limit on long-term investments reduced to £2m, signalling defensive positioning and LOBO hedging preparation
findings.detail: The council has tightened its limit on investments beyond 366 days to £2m for 2026/27 (substantially reduced from prior years). The council explicitly states this reduction is to: (1) preserve flexibility for a potential 'defeasement' transaction to hedge remaining LOBO loan risk if market conditions warrant, and (2) maintain flexibility to lock in higher rates without constraining liquidity.
findings.matters: More conservative investment positioning indicates awareness of refinancing risk on remaining LOBO loans and desire to maintain tactical borrowing flexibility during uncertain rate environment.
findings.figures: Non-specified investment limit for long-term principal beyond 366 days: £2m (2026/27, reduced)
findings.quote: *Reduced limit to cover 1) option of 'defeasement' transaction on remaining LOBO and 2) flexibility to lock in higher rates without materially impacting on overall liquidity.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rises 16% in one year from £251.7m to £292.2m
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) has grown from £251.7m (forecast at 31 March 2026) to £292.2m in 2026/27, a £40.5m increase in one year. This is driven primarily by the capital expenditure budget increasing 42% from £80.0m to £113.7m, creating the bulk of the new £141m borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Rapid capital programme growth at time of elevated interest rates and constrained finances significantly increases debt service burden and revenue impact; sustainability dependent on continued capital delivery.
findings.figures: CFR growth £251.7m to £292.2m; capital expenditure £80.0m to £113.7m (42% increase)
findings.quote: The Authority has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and will therefore need to borrow in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing strategy continues to avoid peak rates, with explicit timing risk documented
findings.detail: Rather than lock in long-term borrowing at current elevated rates (5.2-5.8% for 10-50 year PWLB), the council plans to continue using short-term borrowing and refinance regularly as rates are expected to fall. The S151 Officer explicitly identifies the risk: if rates do not fall as anticipated, the council may miss the opportunity to lock in lower rates.
findings.matters: This is an active interest rate timing bet; failure would result in unnecessarily high debt costs during period when rates may plateau or reverse.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates 5yr 4.50%, 10yr 5.20%, 25yr 5.80%, 50yr 5.60%; Bank Rate forecast 3.25% by March 2027
findings.quote: Given the elevated rates seen in 2025 we plan to continue using short-term borrowing to meet our need. This strategy, whilst still sound, isn't without risk. Risk that a temporary decline in rates is missed while we wait for clearer signs of trajectory

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Treasury function expanded to Combined Authority and Freeport; capacity flagged as ongoing concern
findings.detail: The treasury team now manages borrowing and investment for the council plus two additional entities (Combined Authority and Freeport). The S151 Officer reports the team has coped with this expanded scope despite personnel changes, but has flagged capacity as remaining under close review, echoing concerns raised in the 2009 Public Interest Report following Iceland bank crisis.
findings.matters: Treasury staff capacity constraints create operational execution risk; stretched teams increase likelihood of error in high-value transactions. Historical precedent shows this was previously a material weakness.
findings.figures: Treasury function expanded to three entities (council plus two); capacity flagged as key issue post-Iceland
findings.quote: The Treasury function has coped admirably with this demanding operational environment despite several personnel changes, supporting not only NELC's treasury management but also that of the new Combined Authority and the Freeport entity. Capacity, a key issue in the 2009 Public Interest Report (post-Iceland), remains under close review.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Negative reserves driven by SEND pressures are permitted only until 2028
findings.detail: The council holds negative reserves resulting from Special Educational Needs and Disabilities cost pressures. Government rules currently permit this, but only until 2028. This time-limited permission is forcing the council to take on additional new borrowing to manage cash flow rather than using reserves to fund capital schemes.
findings.matters: Hard deadline of 2028 means deficit position must be resolved within three years; interim period forces additional debt funding and higher costs. Unresolved, this creates sustainability risk.
findings.figures: Negative reserves permitted until 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Negative reserve positions brought about by SEND pressures, whilst permitted until 2028, have manifested themselves in additional cash requirement, managed through lower overall balances and new borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: £141m of new borrowing required over three years to fund capital programme and debt maturity
findings.detail: The council forecasts it will need up to £141m of new borrowing across 2026/27-2028/29, comprising both the capital programme expansion and £62m of existing loan maturities. Capital expenditure is rising sharply from £80.0m (current forecast) to £113.7m in 2026/27, and external debt is forecast to grow from £185.8m to £226.4m.
findings.matters: Large refinancing requirement at structurally elevated interest rates (4.50-5.80% for PWLB) significantly increases debt service costs and revenue burden; refinancing risk concentrated in period when rates remain uncertain.
findings.figures: £141m new borrowing required 2026/27-2028/29; capital expenditure £80.0m to £113.7m; existing maturities £62m; external borrowing £185.8m to £226.4m
findings.quote: In total the Authority will need up to £141m of new borrowing assuming the Capital Programme is delivered as forecast over the next three years.

findings.paper_title: 7. Treasury Management Policy and Strategy
findings.headline: Auditor's Value for Money qualification lifted, restoring market borrowing access
findings.detail: The council had been unable to access commercial borrowing from banks and insurance companies due to an audit qualification on its Statement of Accounts. Removal of this qualification in 2026 restores access to these lenders, providing greater flexibility in sourcing the substantial new borrowing the council requires.
findings.matters: Loss and restoration of market access directly affects which lenders will advance funds and on what terms; material to refinancing strategy during a period of significant new borrowing needs.
findings.figures: n/a
findings.quote: One positive change for 2026/27 is the removal our Auditor's Value For Money qualification in our Statement of Accounts. This restores our access to the wider Market (banks/insurers etc) which can offer us more flexible borrowing arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Business rates scheme changes in 2026/27 introduce new multipliers for retail, hospitality and high-value properties, with uncertain impact
findings.detail: Three-yearly revaluation of rateable values takes effect 1 April 2026 alongside introduction of new multipliers for Retail, Hospitality & Leisure (RHL) and high-value properties over £500k, replacing previous reliefs. Changes managed through transitional reliefs. Council adding additional 15% relief for eligible pubs and live music venues. New scheme coincides with already-declining collection performance.
findings.matters: Uncertain impact on yield. Combined with declining collection rates, represents risk to business rates income forecast.
findings.figures: High-value property threshold £500k; 15% additional relief for eligible pubs and venues; new baseline reset
findings.quote: This includes the regular three-yearly revaluation of business rateable values and the introduction of new multipliers for Retail, Hospitality & Leisure (RHL) and high-value properties (over £500k), which will replace previous reliefs in the RHL sector.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council using capital receipts flexibility to fund revenue transformation costs, a non-sustainable financing source
findings.detail: As in prior year, council is applying government's flexibility to use capital receipts towards funding revenue costs of transformation. This is a one-off financing mechanism that cannot continue once capital receipts are exhausted or needed for capital investment. It helps balance revenue budgets now but masks underlying gap.
findings.matters: Non-sustainable financing source masks structural budget challenge. Reduces capital available for investment. When exhausted, budget gap re-emerges.
findings.figures: Amount not specified in this section
findings.quote: As in 2025/26, the Council intends to utilise the Government's flexibility to apply capital receipts towards funding the revenue costs of transformation and change.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Children's services rated Good in July 2025 ILACS inspection, with Outstanding leadership
findings.detail: Recent Ofsted improvement grading follows restructured staffing, new sufficiency strategy to reduce reliance on high-cost external placements, and new case management system. Council plans continued improvement. This is genuine positive movement in a historically pressured service area, which should moderate cost growth going forward.
findings.matters: Children's services was a major cost pressure and audit concern; improvement is material risk reduction for future years. Cost management should improve if improvement trajectory continues.
findings.figures: July 2025 rating; Good service, Outstanding leadership
findings.quote: The July 2025 ILACS inspection, where children's services were graded as Good, with Outstanding leadership.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Three-year settlement with Fair Funding Review benefit phased in at one-third per year through 2028/29
findings.detail: Settlement confirms 6.1% cash increase in funding overall, but this masks uneven distribution. Fair Funding Review (FFR) allocates only one-third of increased funding each year until full amount received in 2028/29. This provides medium-term planning visibility but creates cliff risk if settlement does not extend beyond 2029.
findings.matters: Clarity is good but dependent on continuation beyond 2028/29. Council must plan for potential loss of phased FFR benefit if multi-year settlement not extended.
findings.figures: 6.1% cash increase overall; one-third FFR benefit allocated each of 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29
findings.quote: However, the full benefit of the FFR will be phased in over the settlement period, with approximately one third of the increased funding allocated each year until the full amount is received in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council raising council tax and social care precept at maximum permitted levels, limiting future revenue-raising headroom
findings.detail: Council is applying 2.99% increase to base council tax (at 3% referendum limit) and 2% Adult Social Care precept (maximum available). Combined these raise £80.2M core council tax and £16.6M ASC precept for 2026/27. Council tax base growth is minimal: only 8.9 band D equivalent new properties yielding £17k. By maximizing current-year levers, council has limited flexibility for revenue growth in future.
findings.matters: Council tax and precepts are now ceiling income sources for this council. Future budget gaps cannot be filled from council tax; must come from spending cuts or other income.
findings.figures: £80.2M core council tax; £16.6M ASC precept; 2.99% increase plus 2% precept; tax base growth £17k on minimal property growth
findings.quote: The ASC precept will raise a total of £16.6M in 2026/27 which will mitigate increased social care demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Adult social care demand and complexity continue to increase, requiring sustained transformation focus
findings.detail: Council identifies adult social care as the key area of demand and cost pressure going forward: both volume and complexity of need are rising. This is being addressed through transformation plans, but transformation is not guaranteed to match pace of demand. ASC is now funded partly through precept (£16.6M from 2% social care precept in 2026/27) and partly from core grant allocation.
findings.matters: Ongoing cost driver that rises regardless of council actions. Complexity particularly matters as it increases cost per case. A finance director must track whether transformation is keeping pace.
findings.figures: ASC precept raising £16.6M in 2026/27; core allocation to be confirmed
findings.quote: Continued transformation and targeted change will be essential to ensure the Council achieves the right outcomes and maintains financial sustainability over the medium term, particularly in Adult Social Care, where both demand and complexity are increasing.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council increasing reserve contributions in 2026/27 to buffer transformation period and ongoing uncertainty
findings.detail: Council is building reserves above normal levels, explicitly stating this reflects the 'current period of transformation and ongoing uncertainty.' This is a precautionary measure signalling the council's own assessment of risk in delivering its plans—acknowledging execution risk exists even as it plans for success.
findings.matters: Reserve building can smooth shocks but also signals underlying uncertainty. A council building reserves while claiming a balanced budget is hedging its bets on plan delivery.
findings.figures: Increase in net reserve contributions proposed but amount not specified in this section
findings.quote: The proposed increase in net contributions to reserves for 2026/27 reflects the current period of transformation and ongoing uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Business rates collection fell during 2025/26; forecasting challenging in current economic environment
findings.detail: Collection performance was below prior-year levels at mid-2025/26. With businesses facing rising costs and smaller firms particularly affected, forecasting is difficult. Council maintains Business Rates Reserve to smooth volatility. Rates are material income: approximately £54.6M forecast for 2026/27, around 25% of total revenue funding.
findings.matters: Declining collection is a cash risk that may require reserve draws. Business rates are the second-largest income source after council tax.
findings.figures: £54.6M forecast 2026/27; collection rate challenged; reserve held to manage swings
findings.quote: Collection performance for Business Rates was slightly reduced against previous years as at the mid-point of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Budget is balanced for 2026/27-2028/29 but dependent on successful delivery of transformation plans
findings.detail: The council explicitly states the balanced position is conditional: 'not without risk and is dependant on the successful delivery of ambitious business and transformation plans.' Transformation is particularly needed in Adult Social Care (demand and complexity rising) and Children's Services (though recently rated Good). The budget cannot balance without execution of planned changes.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to distinguish between structural balance and balance dependent on uncertain future delivery. This budget is the latter.
findings.figures: 2026/27-2028/29 budget periods affected
findings.quote: Both the 2026/27 budget and future years are balanced, but this position is not without risk and is dependant on the successful delivery of ambitious business and transformation plans to secure long-term financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 9. Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 revenue forecast £1.5m overspend indicates underlying demand-led spending pressures not fully resolved
findings.detail: The council recovered from Q3 2024/25 forecast overspend of £0.9m to a balanced outturn through management action on Children's Services including staffing reconfiguration, renewed sufficiency strategy to reduce high-cost external placements, and new case management system implementation. However Q1 2025/26 forecast presented to Cabinet in August 2025 shows £1.5m projected overspend against budget. Early-year overspend suggests the underlying structural cost drivers in demand-led services (particularly children's and social care) remain unresolved despite 2024/25 recovery measures.
findings.matters: The return to overspend forecast in the new financial year, despite recovery actions taken in 2024/25, signals that spending pressures remain structural rather than one-off. Early-year overspends typically cascade through the financial year. This is material context for lenders and peer councils managing similar social care cost pressures.
findings.figures: Q3 2024/25 forecast overspend £0.9m; 2024/25 outturn balanced; Q1 2025/26 forecast overspend £1.5m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Quarter 1 forecast revenue position, presented to Cabinet in August 2025 has the Council forecasting an overspend of £1.5m against budget, it does not currently indicate a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 9. Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued 22 December 2025 on 2024/25 financial statements with no material misstatements identified
findings.detail: The auditors issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, confirming they give a true and fair view without qualification. Draft accounts were received on 30 June 2025 (ahead of statutory deadline) and assessed as of good quality with comprehensive working papers. Three significant audit risks (management override, valuation of land and buildings/investment properties, pension valuation) were satisfactorily addressed with no material issues. Auditors encountered no significant difficulties and noted full cooperation from management.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion confirms the reliability of financial statements for assessing the council's financial position. Against the backdrop of DSG deficits, children's services investment, and staffing challenges, a clean audit indicates sound financial governance and accounting practices.
findings.figures: Audit opinion issued 22 December 2025; draft accounts submitted 30 June 2025; three significant risks all satisfactorily addressed with no material misstatements
findings.quote: Our audit report, issued on 22 December 2025 gave an unqualified opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 9. Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant outturn overspend of £7.95m driven by High Needs Block with statutory override protection extended to March 2028
findings.detail: The 2024/25 DSG outturn shows an overspend of £7.95m, primarily driven by High Needs Block pressures. This is part of a cumulative DSG deficit growing across the sector. The Government's statutory override (which defers incorporation of DSG deficits into councils' useable reserves) was extended from its original March 2026 expiry to March 2028. On expiry, the cumulative deficit must be incorporated into reserves with severe impact on sustainability. Auditors acknowledge this is a major national issue but stress the council must work with partners on comprehensive mitigation planning.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent one of the most significant structural financial challenges in English local government. The override extension provides time, but only to March 2028. After that, the cumulative deficit becomes a direct liability on reserves. Lenders and peer councils are monitoring how this sector-wide issue will be resolved.
findings.figures: £7.95m DSG outturn overspend 2024/25; statutory override extended to 31 March 2028 (from 31 March 2026); described by auditors as a major national issue impacting local authorities across the country
findings.quote: On expiry of the override, the Council would need to incorporate the cumulative deficit in its useable reserves, which would have a significantly detrimental impact to the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 9. Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: OFSTED reassessment of children's services from Inadequate to Good in July 2025 removes prior significant governance weakness
findings.detail: The council faced a prior-year significant weakness following OFSTED's October 2021 Inadequate rating for children's services, citing weaknesses in assessment, planning and decision-making. A full OFSTED inspection in July 2025 rated children's services as Good overall and Outstanding for impact of leaders on social work practice. The auditors are satisfied the improvement was evident throughout 2024/25 based on interim monitoring, and confirm the significant weakness can now be lifted. The council invested significantly through flexible capital receipts and earmarked reserves to fund the service transformation.
findings.matters: Removal of a significant governance weakness materially improves the council's risk profile. For peer finance directors, demonstrates that targeted investment in service transformation can address inspection findings and institutional risk.
findings.figures: OFSTED inspection July 2025; prior 2021 rating Inadequate; July 2025 rating Good overall and Outstanding for leadership impact
findings.quote: In July 2025 OFSTED completed an Inspection of North East Lincolnshire's local authority children's services, and has now reported its findings. The overall assessment was Good in all areas, except for the impact of leaders on social work practice with children and families, which was rated as Outstanding.

news_drafts.headline: North East Lincolnshire confirms dedicated schools grant high needs stability grant after SEND plan approved
news_drafts.lead:
North East Lincolnshire Council has received confirmation of a high needs stability grant from the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, after its reform plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) was approved. The Scrutiny Panel for Health and Adult Social Care considered the update in the council's quarter 2 Council Plan performance and finance report on 25 November 2026.

High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The report lists the stability grant as an additional source of certainty alongside the multi-year settlement. It says the council "has received confirmation of a DSG high needs stability grant following approval of is reform plan."

The paper gives no figure for the grant, and it does not set out how much the grant is worth, when it is paid or over what period. The report does not say how the grant relates to the council's high needs spending or to any deficit on the schools grant.
news_drafts.paper_title: 7. Quarter 2 Council Plan Performance Finance Report Combined

news_drafts.headline: North East Lincolnshire told of high needs stability grant after its SEND reform plan was approved
news_drafts.lead:
North East Lincolnshire Council has received confirmation of a stability grant for high needs, the part of the dedicated schools grant that funds support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The council's quarter 2 Council Plan performance and finance report, before the Scrutiny Panel - Communities on 19 November 2026, says the grant followed approval of its reform plan.

The paper states that "the Council has received confirmation of a DSG high needs stability grant". The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools. The report gives no figure for the stability grant in this section.

The report sets the grant alongside the multi-year financial settlement and presents the two as greater funding certainty for planning the next three years.
news_drafts.paper_title: 7. Quarter 2 Council Plan Performance Finance Report

news_drafts.headline: North East Lincolnshire forecasts a £1.6m overspend for 2026/27 at quarter 2, with children's and adult services over budget
news_drafts.lead:
North East Lincolnshire Council forecasts a full-year overspend of £1.6m on day-to-day spending at quarter 2, according to the finance report to its cabinet on 11 November. The paper describes this as a modest improvement on the quarter 1 forecast.

Service budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.9m. Corporate budgets are forecast to come in at £0.9m against a revised budget of £3.2m, a variance of £2.3m under budget. The paper says the underlying position remains challenging.

Within services, Children and Family Services is forecasting a £4.7m overspend and Adult Services a £3.2m overspend. The paper attributes the social care pressures to demand above budget assumptions, high-cost placements and increasing complexity of need. It names Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out support for children with special educational needs, as a particular source of demand.
